Of the development runs whose saved designs were rebuilt on Vivado 2026.1, 6 reached routing; setup slack was positive in 6.

rows.summary: MMCM VCO is 600-1200 MHz on a -1 7-series part but 800-1600 MHz on the K26; a ZU+ multiplier can be illegal on Artix-7.
7-series PLLE2 is a general clock generator; the UltraScale+ PLLE4 has no external feedback or deskew and is meant for I/O PHY clocking.
BUFR, BUFIO, BUFMR and BUFH exist only on 7-series; UltraScale+ uses BUFGCE, BUFGCE_DIV, BUFG_GT and BUFG_PS, and synthesis maps BUFG to BUFGCE.
A 7-series clock region spans half the device width; UltraScale+ regions are fixed-size tiles with segmented routing and distribution tracks, controlled with CLOCK_ROOT.
7-series has MRCC/SRCC clock-capable pins; UltraScale+ has GC pins on HP banks and HDGC pins on HD banks, and HDGC reaches only BUFGCE.
MMCME4 can change an output divider without a reset (CDDC); MMCME2 output changes need the DRP and a reset or relock.
Vivado retargets some 7-series clocking primitives on UltraScale+: an MMCME2_ADV in RTL synthesises to MMCME4_ADV, but the VCO limits then follow the new part.
CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE values differ: 7-series takes TRUE, BACKBONE or FALSE; UltraScale+ adds SAME_CMT_COLUMN and ANY_CMT_COLUMN, which 7-series does not have.

gaps: The Clocking Wizard's own settings were compared with the flow's search on only a few target frequencies.

rows.summary: Artix-7 and the Zynq-7020 have only HR banks (1.2-3.3 V); the K26 has HP banks (1.8 V maximum) and HD banks (up to 3.3 V).
IDELAYE2 has 32 taps of about 78 ps at a 200 MHz reference; IDELAYE3 has 512 taps of 2.1-12 ps and a TIME mode that holds a delay in picoseconds across voltage and temperature.
ISERDESE2/OSERDESE2 take widths up to 8 (14 cascaded) with BITSLIP; UltraScale+ ISERDESE3/OSERDESE3 take 4 or 8 with no bitslip, and native mode (RX/TX_BITSLICE) is a different design style.
On HR banks LVDS_25 outputs need VCCO 2.5 V and DIFF_TERM; on UltraScale+ HP banks LVDS runs at 1.8 V with DIFF_TERM_ADV, plus ODT and PRE_EMPHASIS that 7-series lacks.
Artix-7 has GTP transceivers (none on the Nexys A7 part) and the Zynq-7020 has none; the K26 has GTH transceivers with different wizards and reference-clock buffers.
7-series slices have CARRY4 and MUXF7/F8; UltraScale+ CLBs have one CARRY8 and MUXF9, and a 7-series CARRY4 instance has no ZU+ lib cell.

Artix-7 and the ZU+ PL have no hard Ethernet MAC: a fabric MAC drives a PHY through SelectIO (RMII, MII, RGMII). Both Zynq PS families have hard GEMs: RGMII through MIO, GMII through EMIO to PL logic.
RGMII's DDR registers are IDDR/ODDR on 7-series and IDDRE1/ODDRE1 on UltraScale+; both have a same-edge-pipelined input mode, but ODDRE1 has no opposite-edge mode.
Both families have 32-, 64-, 128- and 256-deep single-bit LUT RAMs; UltraScale+ adds RAM32M16, RAM64M8, RAM256X1D and RAM512X1S, so wide multi-port shapes and 512-deep columns exist only there.

rows.summary: UltraRAM (288 Kb, 4K x 72, one clock) exists on the K26 (64 blocks) but on no 7-series part; ram_style ultra has nothing to map to on Artix-7.
RAMB36E2 cascades data in the BRAM column (CASCADE_ORDER) with no fabric logic; RAMB36E1 only pairs two halves for a 64K x 1 memory.
Both families have 64-bit ECC in a RAMB36 in SDP mode; only RAMB36E2 adds an ECC pipeline register (EN_ECC_PIPE) for higher clock rates.
FIFO36E2 is not backward compatible with FIFO36E1: reset becomes synchronous, flag latencies change and asymmetric widths appear.
PL DRAM on Artix-7 uses MIG for DDR2/DDR3 on HR banks; the K26 uses the PS DDR4 controller, and a PL DDR4 controller (PG150) needs HP banks.
Both PS families have 256 KB OCM, but its address map and PL access path differ (Zynq-7000 through the GP/ACP ports, ZU+ through HPM/HPC/ACP and the LPD).

gaps: No committed run exercises error correction, dual-port or asynchronous memory behaviour in Vivado or on hardware; the skills give the rules.
The memory controller's pin validation lives in the GUI and has no script command, so pins are checked against rules instead; that rule checker is not in this repository yet.
The choice of DDR device, count, width and speed rests on the skills alone; no memory-interface design has been run.

areas.about: Finite state machines carry the control in most designs. The skills cover separating control from counters, what a register on an input or an output costs in latency and timing, choosing an encoding and a reset (including a reset inside a clock-enable branch), running a slow machine on one fast clock, and checking that the tests reach every state and every legal transition. The coverage check is an evidence file that the flow can add to the second verification stage; it is off unless asked for.

checks.what: Synchronous-reset rule, no latch and no combinational loop; part of the standards stage gate that covers all RTL.
Reads the state register's value changes against the machine's state table: every state visited, every legal transition taken, none outside the table. Off unless the flag is given.
An input launched by another clock must pass two synchroniser registers; a direct use or a single register is flagged.

evidence.text: One controller built in Vivado two ways with the same behaviour: 11 states plus a counter (29 LUTs) and 23 states with the counter folded in (24 LUTs). Folding was the smaller; the split machine has 13 transitions to cover instead of 39.

At the test clock the slack from the state flops to an output pin was -1.859 ns with a decoded output and -0.437 ns with a registered one. A registered decode adds 1 clock of latency; registering the decode of the next state adds 0.

A state machine on a one-in-N clock enable, constrained with the multicycle pair on its own registers: slack between its registers was -0.659 ns without the exception and 1.283, 6.267 and 16.359 ns at three enable ratios.
The coverage check passed on 3 designs with their real tests, and failed, naming the missed state or transition, in 3 of 3 runs with one test removed.
A hand-built lift controller, a state machine with timers, passed its self-check on the board in 1 of 1 run.

Two checks in the power-closure stage gate enforce it: the junction temperature Vivado computes for the board's real cooling must stay within the limit, and the total on-chip power and temperature must fit the budget for the board's power source, which the board tools check again before programming.

Part of the power-closure stage gate: total on-chip power and junction temperature must be within the limits for the board's power source, and the board tools refuse to program a build that fails.
